questions.question: Explain, using tooth counts, why a 10-tooth driver turning a 30-tooth driven gear makes the driven gear turn more slowly, and state by how much.
questions.expected_answer: Teeth pass the contact point one at a time, so in one full turn the 10-tooth driver moves 10 teeth past the contact point and the 30-tooth driven gear must also move 10 teeth, which is only one third of its rim. The driven gear therefore makes one third of a turn for each turn of the driver: three times slower, a velocity ratio of 1:3.

questions.question: State the relationship between the velocity ratio and the force ratio of a gear pair and explain why it must hold.
questions.expected_answer: They are inverses: velocity ratio up means force ratio down, and the two multiply to 1. A pair with velocity ratio 1:3 has a force ratio (mechanical advantage) of 3:1. This must hold because gears cannot create energy; whatever is gained in speed is lost in turning force and whatever is gained in force is lost in speed, like a long lever or ramp trading distance for force.

questions.question: A learner's PAT model needs a slow, strong lift driven by a hand crank. Describe the gear pair you would choose, state its approximate velocity and force ratios, and give one downside of choosing a much larger ratio.
questions.expected_answer: Choose a small driver on the crank and a large driven gear on the lifting axle, for example 12 teeth driving 36 teeth: velocity ratio 1:3 (output three times slower) and force ratio 3:1 (three times the turning force). A much larger ratio would make the lift very slow, need a driven gear too large to fit the structure or a compound train with more axles, and add friction at every extra mesh.
